blocks.text: …being out and about with respect
Basic understanding and objective 🐕
In forest and field we are guests, and we have a duty to acknowledge all wild animals as hosts to us and our dog.

Any chasing away, unsettling, harassing or even wounding of wild animals by our dog must be prevented. As a dog owner, one has no legal basis for letting a dog run free off the leash in nature if it is not yet reliably under the owner’s leadership.
Not infrequently, letting an untrained dog run free leads to its injury or even death through encounters with the wild animals concerned.
Avoiding unwanted hunting behaviour is therefore a key topic in the training of our dog.

Dogs have a prey drive of varying strength. On the one hand, it is determined by genetic predisposition and, building on that, naturally by imprinting during growing up and the experiences the dog has had.
In principle, the prey drive can be influenced in every dog. The extent to which this succeeds is largely determined by perseverance, consistency and, above all, regular training.
Prey-drive management is based on a strategy of saturation with animal stimuli combined with appropriate behaviour patterns.

Dogs have a prey drive of varying strength – determined by genetic predisposition and by imprinting during growing up. In principle: the prey drive can be influenced in every dog. The extent is largely determined by perseverance, consistency and regular training.
Prey-drive management is based on a strategy of saturation with animal stimuli combined with appropriate behaviour patterns.
Success factors at a glance 📋
Early recognition of hunting behaviour and stimuli.
Appropriate reaction in every situation.
Consistent rules that are reliably kept.
Persistent training over an appropriate period.
Intensive TEAM WALK as the supporting foundation.
Learning and applying the SCOUTING TECHNIQUES.
Applying every individual training stage without skipping any.
Moving on to the next training stage only once the previous one is consolidated.
Important principles ⚖️
With perseverance and intensity, training for prey-drive management is always crowned with success.

The training steps described are applied to the young, growing dog as well as to the adult dog. Ending individual training stages too early, or even skipping them, is not advisable and calls the lasting success of the training into question.
The following applies: the older the dog and the more established its hunting behaviour, the longer and more intensively training must be carried out to achieve the desired change in behaviour.
Preparation and basic attitude 🌲
We go out into open nature with our dog every day, at least every two days. Our dog needs as many sensory impressions of the animal world as possible.
We always move at a calm pace and are relaxed while out. Moving quickly stimulates the urge to hunt.
We need a normal leash, a trailing line of about 6–8 m in length, and a toy or treats.
The contents of the sections TEAM WALK and SCOUTING TECHNIQUES are applied alongside.

lessons.title: Exercise 1 – On the leash and the long trailing line

blocks.text: Procedure and objective 🦮
Depending on the terrain and conditions, we walk our dog on the leash or on the long trailing line. For the time being, there is no longer any unleashed state.
Assuming that our dog is always interested in environmental stimuli, we practise settling into the “down” from the very beginning, wherever we are out and about.

Any stimulus – be it a direct sighting or encounter with wild animals, crossing a fresh game trail, fresh droppings or a still-warm resting place – serves us as training and must necessarily be used to carry out the desired “down”.
The daily quota is initially 10, later regularly 20 to 30 times “down” in the terrain, spread across our tour(s). With a higher number of encounters and stimuli, of course correspondingly more often.
The down procedure follows strictly the guidelines from the sections BASIC TRAINING-DOWN and OFF-LEASH WORK-DISTANCE INTERRUPTIONS.
It is important that our dog increasingly experiences the “down” not as a tiresome duty but, in combination with the TEAM WALK and SCOUTING TECHNIQUES, as an entirely normal, routine procedure.

Each instance is praised calmly and warmly – after the situation is over and we have brought our dog into the “sit”. He now receives his well-earned treat or toy and may carry it along a stretch of the way with us, playfully.

As reliability increases, we can drop the trailing line more and more often, so that our dog merely drags it behind him. If necessary, we are thus able to secure a situation quickly by grabbing it. At the same time, we are already training ourselves for the next training step.

As soon as, after some weeks of persistent training, our dog goes reliably into the “down” without noteworthy help when game appears, without active help from the leash, and this is demonstrable over at least 20–30 encounters with wild animals, we can move on to the next step.

lessons.title: Exercise 2 – On the short trailing line

blocks.text: Procedure and objective 🔗

We have advanced our training to the point where, when distraction from wild animals and their traces appears, our dog goes reliably into the “down” without noteworthy help from the leash and lets the situation pass.
We need a trailing line of about 4 m without a loop. Only a knot at the free end gives us something to grip. Under no circumstances may the line be able to snag anywhere.
We must be fully aware that our dog will find out quite quickly whether he is on a leash or not. We therefore go through the intermediate step of a short trailing line.
From now on, instead of the long trailing line, this stays on the dog during all tours as soon as we release him from the leash. Our dog now moves freely near us with the line trailing.

If our dog wants to move more than 8–10 m away from us, or if we have even the slightest suspicion of a distraction, we bring our dog into the down position by speaking calmly but firmly with “down”. We should already have a “down” carried out as a precaution and never wait for the dog’s reaction first. The aim is for our dog to learn to routinely go “down” at every wild-animal stimulus. Reliability develops exclusively in this way.

Since carrying and using the short trailing line means no further effort for us and our dog, yet is of outstanding importance for the lasting effect of the training, this training stage extends over at least 4–6 months.
Only once we have achieved the highest possible routine in the reliability of carrying out “down” in the case of sudden distraction by wild animals at this stage can we move on to the final step.

lessons.title: Exercise 3 – Taking the dog off the leash

blocks.text: Procedure and objective 🔓

We have trained ourselves and our dog to the point where, at every distracting stimulus, we calm our dog promptly with a quiet “down” to such an extent that he no longer makes any attempt to set off and reliably lies down for the entire duration of the stimulus.

We walk calmly and relaxed through the terrain with our unleashed dog. We remain attentive and decide responsibly where we can move off the leash and where it is better to keep the dog on the leash, the short trailing line or the long trailing line. Be just as responsible as climbers on rock, who also decide anew each time whether they have to secure each other with ropes or can climb free.
When distracting stimuli appear, we react early and confidently with “down”, which our dog, thanks to weeks of training, now carries out fluently and reliably.
We support our dog by walking towards him when giving the command and, with the hand held low, imitating a grip on the trailing line, which is no longer there.

Over the next weeks, we learn to deal with situations better and better. We notice that it takes less and less effort to bring our dog into the down position, increasingly even when he does want to break away after all.
From now on, we move through the terrain more calmly and continue to use every opportunity for training. Calm, intensive praise ends every situation that has passed.
Important notes ⚠️
In the first weeks, absolutely avoid taking the dog off the leash. Every failed attempt destroys the success of the training in the long term.
Avoid moving to the next exercise stage too early. An exercise stage must be reliably retrievable before one moves on to the next.
Avoid faulty training. It is better to go back one exercise stage and consolidate it than to accept failed attempts and a failure of the training with the next stage.
Avoid training in a distracted state. Always be present and aware in training.
Avoid loud, hectic, unconscious behaviour.
Practical impulse: Patience beats prey drive

Prey-drive management is not a quick fix – it is a long-term process. Use every walk as a training session, never move on to the next stage too early and go back a stage without hesitation if necessary. Nature is your daily training camp – and your dog will thank you with growing reliability.
→ Am I out in the terrain with my dog attentively and free of distraction?
→ Do I have the long training line with me for demanding training stages?
→ Do I keep to a training interval of at least every 2nd day?
→ Do I carry the knowledge learned from TEAM WALK and SCOUTING TECHNIQUES with me?
→ Do I maintain the training state of walking with the long trailing line?
→ Do I condition the “down” with a sufficient number of repetitions?
→ Am I relaxed, and do I convey this to my dog?
→ Do I praise generously after every training situation that went well?
→ Do I only make the switch to the short training line once I have built up confidence in leading?
→ Does the training with the auxiliary lines really extend over a sufficiently long period until the desired training goals are consolidated?
→ Do I recognise when it is advisable to go back a step and consolidate training sequences – and do I remain consistent in training?
